I hadn't previously known about @Cody Roux's name-the-biggest-number Rocq project, but after @Marc Huisinga mentioned it to me I thought we should have it, too.

Bonus points, I think for not jumping too far ahead: don't just try to win, try to do "the next bigger number" after the current "biggest number". That will make it more fun for everyone.

https://github.com/kim-em/name-the-biggest-number is open for PRs. If you follow the rules, your PRs get merged automatically. (The rule enforcement isn't bullet-proof, play nice.)

Awesome! I am very sad I didn't beat the current contender in the Rocq version, it was hard work but would have been feasible.

One reason I didn't really push it in Lean was the classical/intuitionistic distinction, which should qualitatively change the game a bit (e.g. Busy Beaver should come into play quite early now).

That being said it should be fun in Lean! And might give incentive to flesh out computability theory a bit.
One should clarify the rules on constructivity. The repo has @Cody Roux’s original constructivity requirement, but you also allow mathlib.

Is this going to cap out at
"the output of a largest function defined in a strongly normalising calculus with proof theoretic strength of ZFC + finitely many inaccessibles"?

Right. I see 2 easy choices:

  1. require the definition to be computable, but all proofs in the definition and that it is the contender may be classical.
  2. No restrictions on definition or proof (except axioms of course)

More subtle rules could ask that the number be recursive, e.g. or exclude classical axioms (I think that's a bad idea)

Jeremy Chen said:

Is this going to cap out at
"the output of a largest function defined in a strongly normalising calculus with proof theoretic strength of ZFC + finitely many inaccessibles"?

Yes, or a little before. But it's more work than one would expect with an English hand wavy proof.

Indeed proving that that number is larger than the previous ones should be a nice exercise in meta-programing.
definitely a big number. probably bigger than 1 million.

Cody Roux said:

Indeed proving that that number is larger than the previous ones should be a nice exercise in meta-programing.

So this would be, getting <previous contender>, taking its kernel term, determining the maximum universe level it uses, then embed it into your calculus. Definitely a challenge to get in under a minute :)

Yes, basically formalizing Lean with k universes without axioms, and type checking the term.

Not trivial.
I made a PR adding a "small" version of Graham's number (so its still beatable), but some workflow appears to be stuck
@Felix Pernegger, for now I need to approve CI for new contributors. But how about we don't jump ahead? Even G_1 is too big to merely beat 42.

Interesting game! I wonder if it would be a good idea to require small numbers (e.g. below 10↑↑3 in Knuth's notation) to have some sort of special property for submission, in order to avoid submissions consisting of only a long decimal expansion in the meantime. (For example maybe Belphegor's prime would be a notable enough property for a submission?)

I added big numbers (incrementally and some API along the way) "up to" Conway chained arrow notation which dominates Graham's number and is straightforward to calculate.

The next step would probably to add Tree(3) (or possibly Goodstein sequences which I think is harder), which however first needs Kruskal's tree theorem, which in turn has about 2.5 pages proof. After that it becomes kind of hard to find bigger computable numbers
So ... is the TREE(n) can only be defined using Nat.find?
No, but it's difficult to avoid

And frankly I don't know of any nice references for the lower bounds, I'm excited to see if we can actually add TREE(3).

Of course there are much bigger numbers that are easier to add.

At least in Wikipedia page https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kruskal%27s_tree_theorem#TREE_function there is no recursive definition of TREE(n) but only says (equivalently) that TREE(n) + 1 is the smallest number m such that for any sequence of XXX of length m, property YYY holds. There is only finitely many such sequence, and the property is DecidablePred, so the whole thing is DecidablePred, so the whole thing defined using Nat.find is a computable def, unlike busy beaver number.
It's computable for sure yeah, but you don't even need the "slightly non constructive" Nat.find, I think. Small quibble I guess.
But that is sort of "not effectively computable" (discussed by Kevin Buzzard before) in the sense that it does not have a recursively defined upper bound, is it?

Cody Roux said:

It's computable for sure yeah, but you don't even need the "slightly non constructive" Nat.find, I think. Small quibble I guess.

OK I see. So the lazy way to define TREE(n) in Lean is prove Kruskal's tree theorem (classical is permitted) then using Nat.find to define it. What you have proposed is define (an upper bound of?) TREE(n) recursively, right?

Sure, but the proof is similar: you prove well foundedness of the tree relation and just define TREE(n) by well founded recursion using the finiteness of trees of size n. You get the same number, and the definition is very similar.

Felix Pernegger said:

The next step would probably to add Tree(3) (or possibly Goodstein sequences which I think is harder), which however first needs Kruskal's tree theorem, which in turn has about 2.5 pages proof. After that it becomes kind of hard to find bigger computable numbers

This skips a whole lot of steps.

I think a good step in between is to define the fast-growing hierarchy. I'm not sure how quickly Conway's chained arrow notation grows, but it's smaller than fϵ0f_{\epsilon_0}fϵ0​​, right? We actually have this in Mathlib: docs#ONote.fastGrowingε₀. Another nice candidate would be fζ0f_{\zeta_0}fζ0​​ (fff applied to the first fixed point of ϵ\epsilonϵ).
One can also apply the fast growing hierarchy to other interesting ordinals (these are all claimed to be below TREE(3), but I'm not sure how much of it is proven):

  • φω(0)\varphi_\omega(0)φω​(0), see https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Veblen_function
  • Γ0=φ(1,0,0)\Gamma_0=\varphi(1,0,0)Γ0​=φ(1,0,0), see https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feferman%E2%80%93Sch%C3%BCtte_ordinal
  • The small Veblen ordinal, see https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Small_Veblen_ordinal

If you want more ideas of large computable ordinals, I can highly recommend playing this game:
https://olsak.net/mirek/ordinals2/ordinaly.html

(At the university of Bonn there will be an event where some high schoolers that will come and do some "independent research". A project that @Michael Rothgang will supervise is actually exactly this topic: formalize large natural numbers. This topic will be full of spoilers :-)
Beyond TREE(3) you can go a bit further with ordinal collapsing functions and the Bachmann–Howard ordinal
Note: The Goodstein sequence is much smaller; it is on the order of fϵ0f_{\epsilon_0}fϵ0​​.
Kruskal's tree theorem was formalized in a previous version of Lean (2, I think) by @Minchao Wu.

Floris van Doorn said:

Kruskal's tree theorem was formalized in a previous version of Lean (2, I think) by Minchao Wu.

Yeah I figured, it's hard to break new ground in Lean. Still it'd be nice to have again.

Floris van Doorn said:

I think a good step in between is to define the fast-growing hierarchy. I'm not sure how quickly Conway's chained arrow notation grows, but it's smaller than fϵ0f_{\epsilon_0}fϵ0​​, right? We actually have this in Mathlib: docs#ONote.fastGrowingε₀. Another nice candidate would be fζ0f_{\zeta_0}fζ0​​ (fff applied to the first fixed point of ϵ\epsilonϵ).

I had thought about something along these lines, but "the" fast growing-hierachy depends on what sequence you assiocate to each limit ordinal, right (and in particular is not unique)? And probably there is no satisfying solution that works for all ordinals (especially those with uncountable cofinality)?

So probably one would make a general definition when something is a fast growing hierachy and then define various examples of fast growing hierachies?
(Note I also dont wanna scoop high schoolers too much, so we can skip this of course :))
I tried for a while to get general fundamental sequences into Mathlib but I eventually decided against it. It's at most a hobbyist topic you use specific constructions of for very niche arguments.

But the most general computable definition is that you'd have a well-order, and to every element you associate either a length 0 sequence (for 0) or a length 1 sequence (for successors) or a sequence N -> a which is strictly increasing and converges to it. On top of that you can define your SGH or FGH or Hardy Hierarchy or whatever.
Tbh for this large number nonsense you don't really need well-orders, well-founded is more than enough. Not sure about the "hobbyist" remark though. Are proof theorists not mathematicians then?

Yes, from a formal mathematical perspective, the largest drawback for fundamental sequences is that it's very difficult if not outright impossible to compare the growth rates of two different FGHs with different fundamental sequences, even on the same type. And it's very difficult to gauge the size of any specific value. All you really know is that you have an embedding of some countable ordinal into the partial order of N -> N under eventual domination.

Cody Roux said:

Tbh for this large number nonsense you don't really need well-orders, well-founded is more than enough. Not sure about the "hobbyist" remark though. Are proof theorists not mathematicians then?

That's the niche applications I was referring to. From my understanding some proofs do require building specific instances of fundamental sequences up to some ordinal, but these are only auxiliary constructions rather than a focused object of study.
Still, if there is interest in seeing fundamental sequences in Mathlib, I could revive my PRs...

I was investigating large numbers by making games about them, such as

  • Cookie Clicker Ultra -- FGH below epsilon0 (but with a slow start).
  • Ordinaly -- large countable ordinals up to the OCF till the fixpoint of Aleph.

I've put a modernization of it here (thanks to Astra): https://github.com/minchaowu/Kruskal.lean4 Feel free to import if people here find it useful.
